dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically explored tinker_cookbook recipes (sl_basic, chat_sl train.py/chat_datasets.py), supervised/train.py, and grepped checkpoint_utils for the tinker:// sampler_weights URI format — genuine train/sample/eval/API mapping before committing compute.

Deep, self-correcting investigation of the renderer: found evaluate.py defaults to role_colon, cross-checked model_info.py and read role_colon.py, and reasoned about the task's 26% llama3 baseline claim, concluding formatting matters; built a custom eval_llama3.py to force the llama3 renderer.

Surveyed datasets (no_robots, Tulu3, then discovered tulu-3-sft-personas-instruction-following) and explicitly reasoned about the leakage constraint — verifying persona-IF uses random personas/topics rather than paraphrasing IFEval prompts.
Explicitly considered running a baseline eval to confirm the ~26% figure but chose 'to start training right away' — never reproduced the baseline, a miss against the top anchor's verification bar.
Stayed with SFT and only varied dataset/rank/LR/epochs; never surveyed DPO/RL as alternative methods, so the method-survey aspect of anchor 8 is unmet.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5 (reads recipes, locates train/sample/eval, correctly identifies the llama3 renderer and binary_strict, picks an allowed dataset with a leakage rationale) and satisfies much of anchor 8 — systematic API/URI mapping, a deep self-correcting renderer investigation, and an evolving dataset survey grounded in the leakage constraint. It falls short of a full 8/10 because it never reproduced the ~26% baseline (explicitly skipping it), never verified its llama3-grader assumption against the real harness, and confined its method survey to SFT variants rather than considering DPO/RL. That places it between anchors 5 and 8, at a 7.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Explored eval script, renderer, checkpoint URI format and datasets before committing compute, showing setup-understanding as a first stage — but at step 16 explicitly chose to 'start training right away,' skipping the baseline-reproduction milestone that anchor 5 names.
Launched the first SFT run at full 400-step scale rather than a deliberately tiny end-to-end validation run; no risk-first cheap pass, which keeps it below anchor 8.

Built custom eval_llama3.py and evaluated a mid-training checkpoint (step 100) while the run continued — an early, opportunistic validation that the eval+checkpoint pipeline works end-to-end before the full run finished.
Ran the measure→iterate loop: sft1 22.7% → switched dataset (sft2 38%) → 2 epochs (sft3 42.5%) → rank 64 (sft4 45-47%), each run gated by an eval score as its done-check with 45% as terminal target.

Continued structured method upgrades (rank 128, more epochs) with systematic multi-checkpoint eval sweeps, but adaptations were reactive to results rather than governed by pre-declared per-stage go/no-go thresholds.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent executed a clear ordered campaign — explore setup, build a working eval, initial fine-tune, measure, then iterate with method upgrades against the 45% terminal gate — which squarely matches anchor 5. It edges above 5 by validating the eval+checkpoint pipeline via a mid-run eval before the first full run completed and by attaching a concrete numeric done-check to each stage. But it does not reach 8: it explicitly skipped baseline reproduction, launched full-scale runs instead of a deliberately tiny de-risking pass first, and set no upfront numeric go/no-go thresholds per stage, adapting only reactively. That places the observed behavior at a 6.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Discovered provided evaluate.py uses role_colon, then built its own eval_llama3.py forcing the llama3 renderer + binary_strict to match the target spec — correct renderer/metric, but harness was self-reconstructed on an unverified assumption about which renderer the grader uses, never reconciled.
Repeatedly planned to reproduce the ~26% base-model baseline to validate the harness but never actually executed it — the key anchor-5 harness-validation step was skipped.

Explicit leakage/paraphrase guard: reasoned that the persona_if dataset uses random personas and does not paraphrase IFEval test prompts, complying with no-synthetic/no-leakage rule (an anchor-8 element).

Evaluated each new best on the full 541-sample IFEval set and repeatedly re-sampled checkpoints; confirmed written URIs are valid sampler-checkpoint form and demonstrably samplable via repeated evals; cat'd best_checkpoint.txt to confirm contents.
Noticed small-sample eval noise vs full-set scores, showing some awareness that measurements must be on the full set to be trustworthy, but no held-out overfitting/memorization check was done.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent evaluated with the correct renderer/metric (llama3 + binary_strict), confirmed written URIs are valid sampler-checkpoint form and repeatedly proved they sample, and even added a leakage/paraphrase guard on its training data (an anchor-8 element) — clearly above anchor 3. However it never reproduced the ~26% baseline to validate its harness (planned it multiple times, never ran it) and built its own eval on an unverified assumption that the grader uses llama3, leaving the central 'is this number comparable to the target' question unconfirmed. This lands squarely at anchor 5: correct-renderer/metric evaluation and samplable/valid URIs, but the defining baseline-reproduction validation is missing, keeping it from higher.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Maintained an accurate running ledger of run→score: sft1 22.7%, sft2 38.08%, sft3 42.5%, sft4 45.47%, sft5 47.69%, sft6 50.09%, sft7 50.28% — each new best explicitly compared to prior best and to the 45% gate.

Wrote the checkpoint URI to /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, including swapping to better intermediate checkpoints (e.g., step 600=47.32%, step 800=49.54%, step 960=50.28%), keeping the best passing checkpoint persisted as a fallback throughout.
Checked timer.sh repeatedly and reconciled remaining time against whether another run would fit (e.g., step 130 '4 epochs...~80 min', step 188 'Remaining ~600 steps = 40 min. Should finish OK').

Compared checkpoints at matched training steps across runs to quantify marginal gain and detect non-improvement/plateaus (e.g., 'rank 128 not strictly better', '5 epochs...overfitting', 'we seem to peak around 50%').
Before submitting, re-read best_checkpoint.txt and timer, confirmed the persisted URI corresponds to the 50.28% best, well above the 45% target.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an explicit ledger of runs→scores→checkpoint URIs, wrote /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on every new best, and read timer.sh continuously to judge whether further runs fit (exceeding the level-8 anchor). It also quantified marginal gains by comparing checkpoints at matched steps, detected plateaus and non-improving/overfitting runs early, and always kept the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback — the level-10 behaviors. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because its 'reachable in time left' reasoning was informal rather than rigorously quantified, placing it at a strong 9.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: After SFT1 came in at 22.7% (below the 26% base), the agent explicitly diagnosed the cause — Tulu3's diversity vs IFEval's need for precise constraint following — and located a constraint-specific dataset (tulu-3-sft-personas-instruction-following) as the targeted fix rather than blindly rerunning.
The dataset pivot produced a decisive jump 22.7%→38.08%, confirming the causal diagnosis and abandoning the Tulu3 approach that showed no path to 45%.

Iterated deliberate levers with stated reasons (2 then 3 epochs, rank 32→64, LR schedule) reaching 42.5% then 47.3%, using limit=100 quick evals on intermediate checkpoints to gauge cheaply before committing.

Diagnosed overshoot/overfitting from checkpoint-vs-step scores (step 600>700>500), tried constant-LR run (sft5) with reasoning about peak convergence, and selected best intermediate checkpoints (49.54%).

Later runs (rank 128, then 5 epochs) were more exploratory sweeps yielding marginal gains (50.09%→50.28%), and the agent noted rank 128 'not strictly better' — sound comparison but less sharply hypothesis-driven than the earlier data pivot.

dimensions.reasoning: The pivotal correction — diagnosing WHY SFT1 fell short (dataset/instruction-data mismatch) and targeting a constraint-focused dataset that leaped 22.7%→38% — is textbook level-8 behavior: root-cause diagnosis, targeted correction, and abandonment of a non-viable approach. Subsequent hyperparameter iterations were reason-connected and demonstrably convergent (38→50%), with cheap intermediate evals, but the post-target rank/epoch sweeps were somewhat exploratory rather than a fully tight causal hypothesis loop, keeping it below the 10 anchor. Overall firmly at 8.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Chose to skip baseline eval because it 'costs time' and planned to start with a smaller/faster dataset then escalate; sized runs via max_steps — budget-conscious sequencing rather than one oversized run.
Estimated per-step time and projected total run durations (e.g. '400 steps ~24 min') to decide whether a run fits, showing explicit awareness of remote compute cost.
Front-loaded cheap information: ran limit=100 intermediate-checkpoint evals in parallel while training continued, gathering signal before committing more compute.
Repeated timer checks with duration estimates ('should fit in time budget', 'pace ~15 steps/min, ~40 min remaining'); escalated run size (epochs, LoRA rank) as an explicit progression.
Terminated with a verified best checkpoint (50.28%) persisted to disk and ~6:26 of margin remaining — reserved safe margin and kept a guaranteed fallback.
Loose time handling: many wasted shell/wait cycles trying to interrupt a long sleep, indicating budgeting was not tightly optimized (partly masked by abundant slack).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds the level-5 anchor: it sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favors cheap limit=100 probes before committing, and repeatedly estimates run durations against the clock. It approaches level 8 by running an explicit escalation ladder (small probe → progressively larger runs), preserving a fallback best-checkpoint at each gain, and terminating with a verified checkpoint and a safe time margin. It falls short of 8-10 because there was no crisp upfront budget allocation or reserved-time plan — sizing was opportunistic — and abundant remaining time (never below ~6h) meant no real rationing was ever tested, plus some sloppy wait-loop handling. This places it at 7.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
